title: An attack path and its controls
summary: One vulnerable app meets several layers.

steps.n: The attacker uses a vulnerable library to run code in the app container.
A non-root, read only container with dropped capabilities limits what the code can do.
No service account token is mounted, so there is nothing to use against the API.
Without privileged mode the attacker cannot reach the host.
A network policy blocks calls to other services and the metadata endpoint.
A runtime rule fires on the unexpected shell and the team is alerted.

title: Failure and recovery: a leaked token
summary: A long lived token is found and replaced with a bound one.

steps.n: A developer commits a kubeconfig that contains a long lived token.
A secret scanner reports the token within minutes.
Security deletes the service account token secret so the credential stops working.
They confirm which requests used the token and find no unusual activity.
The pipeline now uses a projected token with an audience and expiry.
A pre-commit and a server side scanner reject kubeconfigs.
The incident is written up without blame and training is updated.

title: Granting access the safe way
summary: A narrow role bound to a group.

steps.n: A team asks to restart deployments in their namespace.
The reviewer creates a role with patch on deployments in that namespace only.
The role is bound to the team group, not to individuals.
The API server now allows the patch and denies everything else.
can-i shows yes for patch and no for secrets.
The binding is listed in the quarterly access review.

title: Failure and recovery: privilege escalation
summary: A pods create right was used to reach secrets.

steps.n: A user with only create pods in a namespace submits a pod.
The pod uses a service account that can read secrets across the namespace.
The pod reads secrets and the user gets credentials they were never granted.
An audit rule flags secret reads by an unusual service account.
Security restricts who can use that service account and narrows its role.
They rotate every secret in the namespace.
Admission policy now blocks pods that use privileged service accounts without approval.
The platform team adds a warn label for the restricted standard.
Developers get warnings when they apply pods that break the standard.
They add non-root, drop capabilities and a seccomp profile to the specs.
An audit label records remaining violations for review.
When violations reach zero the label is changed to enforce.
Admission now rejects any pod that breaks the standard.

title: Encrypting existing secrets
summary: Turning on encryption is not enough on its own.

steps.n: The operator creates an encryption configuration with a KMS provider.
The API server starts with the new configuration flag.
New or updated secrets are stored with an encrypted prefix.
The operator reads and replaces every secret so old ones are encrypted too.
The auditor reads a secret directly in etcd and sees ciphertext.
Credentials that were readable before the change are replaced.

title: Isolating a tenant
summary: Layers keep one team away from another.

steps.n: Tenant A receives a namespace and a group bound to a namespaced role.
A default deny policy blocks traffic from other namespaces.
A quota stops one tenant from using all cluster resources.
Restricted standards stop privileged pods and host access.
Code from unknown users runs on a separate pool with a sandboxed runtime.
A quarterly test tries to cross from one tenant to another and must fail.
kube-bench checks the control plane and nodes against the CIS controls.
It reports that anonymous auth is enabled on the API server.
The operator copies the static pod manifest before editing it.
They set anonymous auth to false and keep every file mount intact.
The kubelet notices the manifest change and recreates the API server.
The benchmark now passes that control and the change is recorded.

title: Failure and recovery: a hardening change breaks the API server
summary: A flag points at a file that was never mounted.

steps.n: The operator adds an audit policy flag to the API server manifest.
The kubelet recreates the API server with the new flag.
The API server cannot read the policy file because it was not mounted into the pod.
kubectl fails because the API server is down.
The operator restores the saved manifest and the API server returns.
They add the volume and mount for the policy file and apply the change again.
Audit events appear and the change process now requires a manifest backup.
A runtime rule reports a shell and an outbound connection from a pod.
The responder changes the pod label so a deny policy cuts its traffic.
The node is cordoned so no new workloads join it.
Logs and the node disk are copied before anything is deleted.
Tokens and secrets that the pod could reach are replaced.
The workload is redeployed from a known good image on a clean node.

title: Failure and recovery: deleting the evidence
summary: A quick pod delete hides the cause and the attacker returns.

steps.n: An attacker runs a miner in a pod through a vulnerable endpoint.
A responder deletes the pod at once to stop the symptom.
The Deployment recreates the same vulnerable pod and the attacker returns.
Security reads the audit log and finds the original request source.
They quarantine the new pod and patch the vulnerable image.
Credentials reachable by the pod are replaced.
The runbook now says contain and preserve before deleting.

title: Finding who did it
summary: Audit events answer who, what and when.

steps.n: An alert reports many secret reads by one account.
The responder filters events by the account and verb.
Events show the source address and the user agent.
The account owner confirms they did not run those commands.
The credential is revoked and the roles are reviewed.
The events are exported to long term storage for the report.
